 Indonesia apologises to ASEAN for haze Indonesia apologises to ASEAN for haze
 Speaking at the 49th ASEAN Summit’s plenary session on Sunday, Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said his administration would hold companies responsible for causing the fires.
 Gembong Hanung
 The Jakarta Post
View all posts by Gembong Hanung → 
 Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (R) welcomes Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto (L) during the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summit retreat sessions in Manila on November 15, 2026. PHOTO: AFP
 November 16, 2026
 JAKARTA – President Prabowo Subianto on Sunday apologized for the haze crisis that has clouded parts of Southeast Asia, as ASEAN leaders met in the Philippines for talks to strengthen cross border enforcement against polluters.
 The 49th ASEAN Summit kicked off with world leaders gathering in Manila to discuss trade, security and an ongoing energy crisis with the bloc, which forms the world’s fifth largest economy.
 Among the most anticipated issues were the wildfires in Indonesia that have sent dense plumes of smoke across national borders and caused tensions between Jakarta and its neighbors.
 Speaking at the summit’s plenary session on Sunday, Prabowo said his administration would hold companies responsible for causing the fires.
 “We’ve revoked 17 concessions [permits] from companies. [Meanwhile] 26 companies are currently under investigation and 11 others have been charged. Another 23 companies are on the list to be charged,” he said, as quoted from a press release from the Presidential Secretariat. “In total, 104 companies are currently under investigation by our police.”
 “We have [also] deployed 71,000 forest firefighters. We lost 16 people who died and many more who were injured while battling the blazes. We also lost two helicopters,” Prabowo said, adding that Indonesia is preparing for the establishment of a new agency and programs to prevent forest fires.
 Prabowo’s remarks came as the problem of transboundary haze has started to disappear.
 The ASEAN Specialized Meteorological Center (ASMC) issued on Nov. 12 a “no transboundary smoke haze” notice for southern parts of Southeast Asia, ending the months-long plumes of haze observed between August and October. The easing of pollution has been linked to recent showers and subdued fire hot spots in Sumatra and Kalimantan.
 Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told a press briefing later on Sunday that Indonesia was “very frank and candid in expressing the efforts they have been exerting in addressing the forest fires in Indonesia” during the plenary session.
 “The [ASEAN] leaders also encouraged member states to prioritize the ratification of the ASEAN Coordinating Center on Transboundary Haze Control [ACC-THPC],” she added.
 Mandated under the 2002 ASEAN Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution, the center is intended to facilitate information-sharing and emergency assistance among member states, coordinating efforts to monitor, prevent and respond to forest fires. Only Vietnam has so far ratified the agreement.
 Speaking at the retreat session later on Sunday, Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong proposed expanding a joint task force the city-state established with Jakarta in October into a region-wide platform, The Strait Times reported.
 The task force was announced on Oct. 27 to coordinate investigations into plantation companies linked to the blazes, including through financial intelligence, cross-border evidence gathering and potential asset recovery.
 Wong also thanked Prabowo on Sunday for calling for investigations, according to The Strait Times.
 Before the summit, Foreign Minister Arrmanatha Nasir met with his Malaysian and Singaporean counterparts on Friday to discuss the growing concerns over the haze pollution.
 “At the trilateral meeting, the foreign ministers of Malaysia and Singapore also welcomed the significant drop in haze conditions,” Arrmanatha’s office said in a statement.
 A day later, ASEAN foreign ministers gathered in Manila and agreed to expedite the operation of the transboundary haze control center, according to Philippine minister Lazaro.
 Jakarta ‘holds the key’ 
 Amplified by the El Niño climate pattern, the latest episode of transboundary pollution has resulted in health problems, school closures and flight cancellations, including in Singapore and Malaysia.
 ASEAN had launched a road map for a haze-free ASEAN by 2020 following a major fire season in 2015, though the target was missed and has since been extended to 2030.
 But the scale of the haze crisis this year has raised doubts over ASEAN’s capacity to achieve the goal.
 Heng Kiah Chun of Greenpeace Malaysia called on ASEAN nations to stop treating haze as an “annual emergency”, while pushing for greater corporate transparency and cross-border enforcement.
 The 2030 target, he added, should be an opportunity for the bloc to prove that “they are serious about ending” the recurring crisis.
 “But without strong enforcement, corporate accountability and concrete action to address deforestation and peatland destruction, this road map risks becoming another promise on paper,” Chun told The Jakarta Post on Sunday.
 Hikmahanto Juwana, an international law professor at the University of Indonesia, said Jakarta “holds the key” to facilitating regional participation in wildfire handling and to enforcing sanctions against errant companies.
 “The key to success is consistent and firm legal enforcement by Indonesia against those involved in forest burning,” he said.
